<meta>The transcription provided is of the title page for Girolamo Menghi's "Compendio dell' Arte Essorcistica." The shelfmark and library stamps mentioned in the OCR meta-data are typical of archival copies held in major European libraries. This page sets the formal structure for one of the most famous manuals on demonology in the early modern period.</meta>

# COMPENDIUM
## OF THE EXORCISTIC ART,
### AND THE POSSIBILITY OF THE WONDROUS & stupendous works of Demons, and of Sorcerers;

->With the appropriate remedies for illnesses caused by witchcraft.<-
->By Father <term>Girolamo Menghi</term><note>Girolamo Menghi (1529–1609) was a Franciscan friar and the most famous exorcist of his time. His writings standardized the practice of exorcism in the Catholic Church for centuries.</note> of Viadana<-
-><term>Observant Friar Minor</term>.<note>A branch of the Franciscan Order that sought to follow the Rule of St. Francis with strict "observance."</note><-

->A work no less useful to Exorcists than<-
->delightful to the Reader, for the common benefit,<-
->newly published.<-

To the right of this central image is a separate ink stamp of a cross surmounted by a crown.</image-desc>

->IN BOLOGNA,<-
->By Giovanni Rossi 1576.<-

->*With the permission of the Superiors.*<note>original: "Con licenza de' Superiori." This indicates the book had passed ecclesiastical censorship and was authorized by the Church.</note><-

<meta>This page follows the title page of Girolamo Menghi's "Compendio dell' Arte Essorcistica" (1576). It contains a commendatory sonnet addressed to the author. The bleed-through mentioned in the source metadata refers to the title "COMPENDIO" from the preceding page.</meta>

# GIULIO NUTI OF BORGO
## SAN SEPOLCRO,
### TO THE AUTHOR.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting floral and vine motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>
Celestial spirit, who teaches us 
How the deeply hidden deceptions 
Of the infernal ones—which cause 
Grave damage among us—may be fled 
By wretched mortals:

You, with gravity, and with swift wings, 
Have descended down to the <term>Tartarean thrones</term>;<note>original: "tartarei scanni." In Renaissance literature, "Tartarean" refers to Tartarus, the deepest abyss of Hades in Greek mythology, here used to describe the seats or realms of Hell.</note> 
And the filthy, wicked tyrants have well seen 
How much you can do, how much you know, and what you are worth.

A clear sign appears to us, that all of them united 
Have not turned you away from such a noble undertaking, 
Which teaches us fully the way to avoid them.

How can the flesh and the world put up a fight, 
If the wicked spirits flee in terror 
From your work, which I revere and praise?

<summary>This page features a commendatory sonnet by Giulio Nuti of Borgo San Sepolcro, praising Girolamo Menghi's spiritual authority and his success in revealing the hidden dangers of the demonic realm.</summary>
<keywords>Giulio Nuti, Girolamo Menghi, sonnet, praise, demonology, Tartarus, spiritual warfare, 16th-century poetry</keywords>

# TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS
## AND MOST REVEREND
## MONSIGNOR, THE LORD
## GIULIO FELTRIO
## DELLA ROVERE,
## MOST MAGNIFICENT CARDINAL,
### And of the entire Franciscan Order
### Most worthy and
### most vigilant Protector.

*BEFORE I came to petition your Most Illustrious Lordship* <note>V. S. Ill.ma (Vostra Signoria Illustrissima): a standard formal honorific for high-ranking nobility and clergy in the 16th century.</note> *to receive this little book* <note>original: "libretto." Authors often used this modest term when dedicating their work to a powerful patron.</note> *under the protection of your name, I ought to provide some reason, as I, who am not even known by name—*

<summary>This page contains the formal dedication of Girolamo Menghi's exorcism manual to Cardinal Giulio della Rovere, the Protector of the Franciscan Order. The author begins his humble address to the Cardinal, seeking patronage for his "little book."</summary>

known by your Lordship, without first providing some knowledge of myself; and that I have taken such boldness; but my excuse lies with you—that is, in your greatness, which even by those of whom you have never heard mention is nonetheless observed and revered. In short, I consider that among all the qualities I possess, there is none that is not less than <note>In this context, "mediocre" reflects the author's performance of humility, suggesting his talents are unremarkable or middling.</note> mediocre, save for that affection and reverence which I bear—both out of <term>obligation</term> <note>original: "obligo"; referring to his duty as a member of the Franciscan Order to his Protector.</note> and by <term>choice</term> <note>original: "elettione"; implying a voluntary personal devotion alongside his official duty.</note>—toward your most noble name. Therefore, setting aside other matters (as unworthy of your attention), I say only this: that just as I am one of those <term>Franciscans</term> <note>Members of the Order of Friars Minor, for whom the Cardinal served as official Protector at the Roman Curia.</note> who live under your most fortunate protection, so I am one of those who feel most particularly indebted to **GOD** for being under such a blessed and glorious <term>Banner</term> <note>original: "Vessillo"; a metaphor for the Cardinal’s leadership and the protection his "coat of arms" provides the Order.</note>. Nor is there anything in the world I desire more than to employ myself (should the opportunity ever arise) in ser-

<summary>In this portion of the dedication, Girolamo Menghi humbles himself before Cardinal della Rovere, claiming his only worthy trait is his devotion to the Cardinal's name. He expresses deep gratitude for being a Franciscan under the Cardinal's "glorious banner."</summary>

<keywords>humility, Franciscan Order, patronage, Giulio della Rovere, 16th-century rhetoric, religious hierarchy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dedication to Cardinal Giulio Feltrio della Rovere, following the author’s expression of desire to serve the Cardinal. The text picks up from the previous page, completing the word "servir" (to serve).</meta>

ving you. It is true that while my own weakness takes away the hope of being able to serve you at your command, I will at least, of my own accord, ensure that my prayers (however cold <note>A common rhetorical gesture of humility, suggesting the author's prayers lack the spiritual heat or worthiness of a more holy person.</note> they may be) are always directed to **GOD** for your happiness—under which I also live. Whereas I should perhaps provide reasons why I dedicate this work to you; but of those two things which those who dedicate their works to others usually do—either narrating the reasons why they are moved to dedicate, or magnifying the greatness of those to whom they dedicate—it seems to me, my Most Illustrious <term>Patron</term> <note>original: "Patrone"; the Cardinal acting as a legal and spiritual guardian for the author and his Order.</note>, that neither remains possible for me, or at least appropriate to be done. For as to the first, since the whole world knows the <term>Protection</term> <note>original: "Protettione"; the formal office of "Cardinal Protector" who represented the Franciscans' interests at the papal court.</note> that you hold over our <term>Order</term> <note>original: "Ordine"; the Franciscan Order (Friars Minor).</note>, it would rather be necessary to give reasons why any one of us would have the boldness to dedicate his works to anyone else. And as for the second, if I were to convince myself that I could...

<summary>Girolamo Menghi argues that a formal justification for this dedication is unnecessary, as the Cardinal's role as the official Protector of the Franciscans makes him the natural recipient of their works. He continues his display of humility, claiming his prayers are "cold" and his ability to praise the Cardinal is limited.</summary>

<keywords>Girolamo Menghi, Cardinal Giulio Feltrio della Rovere, Franciscan Order, patronage, Cardinal Protector, humility, religious dedication</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication to Cardinal Giulio Feltrio della Rovere. The opening fragment "tere" completes the verb "descrivere" (to describe) from the previous page, where the author began explaining why he will not attempt to list the Cardinal’s many virtues.</meta>

...to describe them with the darkness of my words, adding light to the sun, I believe I would cause laughter, or at least provide a very great occasion to be deemed reckless. So, setting aside both of these duties; now, sending forth this little book on the subject of <term>Demons</term> <note>original: "Demoni". The author, Girolamo Menghi, was one of the most influential exorcists of the 16th century.</note> and <term>Spells</term> <note>original: "Malefici"; this refers to harmful magic, sorcery, or the supernatural means by which demons afflict humans.</note>, driven truly by the desire to be of use, I dedicate it to you, and I aspire for it to go forth adorned and enriched by your name; it appearing to me not only fitting on my part that my labors <note>original: "sudori", literally "sweats"; a common Renaissance metaphor for the intense effort of writing and study.</note> be addressed to my **Patron** and **Protector**, but also that on the part of the book itself—it being nothing other than an armory (so to speak) against the assaults of the **Devil** and his ministers—it is further fitting that it should not fall into any other hands than those of a most great and principal soldier of **CHRIST**, and a Prince not only in temporal matters of vast states, but in spiritual matters as well for a great part of the <term>Christian militia</term> <note>original: "Christiana militia"; a concept describing the Church and its members as an army in a perpetual spiritual war against evil.</note>; praying you...

<summary>Girolamo Menghi explains that his book on exorcism is an "armory" against the Devil, making Cardinal della Rovere—a "soldier of Christ"—its most appropriate recipient. He justifies the dedication by citing the Cardinal's dual role as both a secular prince and a spiritual leader.</summary>
<keywords>Girolamo Menghi, Cardinal Giulio Feltrio della Rovere, exorcism, spiritual warfare, patronage, demons, Christian militia</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page concludes the dedication to Cardinal Giulio Feltrio della Rovere. It follows the author's request for the Cardinal to accept the book as a spiritual "armory."</meta>

...that you do not take it ill if I have taken this boldness to offer you this very small sign of my servitude; since he who does what he can remains excused. In short, let the affection found within me make up for the smallness of the gift, and may <term>Your Most Illustrious Lordship</term> <note>original: "Vostra Signoria Illustrissima"; a standard formal address for a high-ranking church official like a Cardinal.</note> accept it (I beseech you) with that readiness of spirit with which you console and favor, with the greatest wonder, whoever turns to you. In the meantime, I shall remain praying to the Lord that He may preserve Your Most Illustrious Lordship for His Church, and for this our **Religious Order** <note>original: "Religione"; here Menghi refers specifically to the Franciscan Order (Order of Friars Minor), to which he belonged.</note> in particular; to whom I pay my respects, praying for your perpetual happiness.

It follows the conclusion of the dedication to Cardinal della Rovere. # THE MOST AUTHORITATIVE AUTHORS CITED
## WITHIN THIS
### WORK.

**Augustine** <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational theologian for Western Christianity.</note>
**Pope Alexander** <note>Likely referring to Alexander III or Alexander IV, whose decrees were frequently cited in canon law.</note>
**Alexander of Hales** <note>A 13th-century Franciscan scholar known as the "Irrefragable Doctor."</note>
**Antoninus the Archbishop** <note>Saint Antoninus of Florence (1389–1459), a Dominican famous for his works on moral theology.</note>
**Alfonso de Castro** <note>A 16th-century Spanish Franciscan jurist and theologian who wrote extensively against heresy.</note>
**Avicenna** <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose philosophical and medical works were standard texts in European universities.</note> ⁖
**Abbot Bernard** <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a Cistercian leader and mystic.</note>
**Bonaventure** <note>Saint Bonaventure (1221–1274), a Franciscan Cardinal and one of the most important medieval philosophers.</note>
**Cyprian the Martyr** <note>Saint Cyprian (c. 210–258), the Bishop of Carthage and an early Christian writer.</note>
**Theological Compendium** <note>original: "Compendio Theologico"; likely refers to the "Compendium of Theological Truth," a popular handbook of the time often attributed to Hugh of Strasbourg.</note>
**Dionysius the Areopagite** <note>A 5th-century Christian philosopher (now known as Pseudo-Dionysius) whose works on the celestial hierarchy were highly influential.</note>
**Various Councils** <note>Refers to the collective authority of the Ecumenical Councils of the Church.</note>
**John Damascene** <note>Saint John of Damascus (c. 675–749), a Syrian monk who summarized the teachings of the Greek Church Fathers.</note> ⁖
**John Chrysostom** <note>Saint John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an early Church Father known for his powerful preaching.</note>
**John Scotus** <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a premier Franciscan theologian known as the "Subtle Doctor."</note>
**John Cassian** <note>Saint John Cassian (c. 360–435), whose writings on monastic life were foundational for Western spirituality.</note>
**Johannes Nider** <note>A 15th-century German Dominican (c. 1380–1438) whose works on reform and the supernatural were widely read.</note>

**Jerome** <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), best known for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate) and his extensive scriptural commentaries.</note>
**William of Paris** <note>William of Auvergne (c. 1180–1249), Bishop of Paris and a prominent philosopher-theologian who integrated Aristotelian thought with Christian doctrine.</note>
**Hilary the Bishop** <note>Saint Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367 AD), a leading theologian against Arianism, often called the "Hammer of the Arians."</note>
**Josephus the Jew, in the *Antiquities of the Jews*** <note>Flavius Josephus (37–c. 100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian whose works provide crucial historical context for the Second Temple period and early Christianity.</note>
**Isidore the Bishop** <note>Saint Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636 AD), author of the *Etymologiae*, which served as the standard encyclopedia of the Middle Ages.</note>
**Michael Psellos, *On the Nature of Demons*** <note>An 11th-century Byzantine monk and polymath; his work on demonology was highly influential in the West during the late Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note>
***The Hammer of Witches*** <note>original: "Martello de Malefici"; better known by its Latin title *Malleus Maleficarum*. This infamous 15th-century treatise by Heinrich Kramer provided a legal and theological framework for the prosecution of witches.</note>
**Nicholas of Lyra** <note>A 14th-century Franciscan whose literal commentary on the Bible was the most widely used during the late Middle Ages.</note>
**Paul of Burgos** <note>A Jewish convert who became a bishop in the 15th century and wrote influential additions to the biblical commentaries of Nicholas of Lyra.</note>
**Paolo Grillandi** <note>original: "Paolo Ghirlando"; a 16th-century Italian jurist and judge in witch trials whose legal writings shaped the procedures for inquisitorial trials.</note>
**Peter Damian** <note>Saint Peter Damian (c. 1007–1072), a Benedictine monk and cardinal known for his strict asceticism and efforts to reform church morality.</note>
**Peter of Palude** <note>A 14th-century Dominican theologian and Patriarch of Jerusalem, known for his writings on the sacraments and canon law.</note>
**Raymond Lully** <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan philosopher and mystic who developed a logical system, the "Ars Magna," intended to prove Christian truths through reason.</note>
**Silvestro Prierias** <note>Silvestro Mazzolini da Prierio (1456–1523), a Dominican theologian and Master of the Sacred Palace who was one of the first to oppose Martin Luther.</note>
**Thomas Aquinas** <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the "Angelic Doctor" and arguably the most influential philosopher and theologian of the Catholic Church.</note>
**Thomas of Cantimpré** <note>original: "Thomaso Barbantino"; a 13th-century Dominican from the Duchy of Brabant (hence "Barbantino") known for his encyclopedia on the nature of things and lives of saints.</note>
***The Lives of the Holy Fathers*** <note>original: "Vite de’ Santi Padri" (Vitae Patrum); a famous collection of biographies and spiritual teachings from the early Christian monks living in the deserts of Egypt and Syria.</note>

# TABLE OF THE CHAPTERS
## WHICH ARE CONTAINED
### WITHIN THE PRESENT
### WORK.

<image-desc>A large square woodcut initial "C" decorated with floral and foliate patterns.</image-desc>THAT the Demons were first created good, and that through their own most wicked will and pride they became perverse and evil. Chapter I.
page 1

Concerning various and diverse generations and species of Demons, and how they perform all their actions through their intellect and will. Chapter II. 9

Concerning the knowledge <term>scienza: in this Renaissance context, this refers to "scientia," or certain knowledge gained through reasoning, rather than the modern experimental method</term> of Demons, the manner in which they acquire it, and how they differ from us in their way of learning. Chapter III. 19

How Demons know future contingent things <note>Refers to events that are not certain to happen, such as those depending on human free will</note>, including a discussion on whether they can know the secrets and thoughts of our hearts. Chapter IV. 25

Demons learn without composing or dividing. 21 <note>original: "senza componere, ò di uidere." These are technical terms from Aristotelian logic. <term>quiddity: from the Latin 'quidditas', meaning the "whatness" or essential nature of a thing</term>, or definition of the thing, is always true; and it cannot be deceived, just as the sense is not deceived regarding its own proper object, as Aristotle says in the third book of *On the Soul* <note>Aristotle, *De Anima*, Book III. Scholastic philosophers frequently cited this to argue that the intellect, when grasping a simple essence, is as reliable as the eye seeing color.</note>; and this is most true when the intellect knows immaterial quiddities, such that they are either truly and totally understood, or totally ignored by said intellect. In this way, therefore, in the Angelic intellect there can be no error or falsehood by itself, regarding the nature of that intellect; nevertheless, error can accidentally fall upon it, but in a different way than it does in us, who by <term>composing or dividing: the process of forming affirmative or negative propositions (e.g., "the apple is red")</term> come to the knowledge of nature and quiddity, or definition—as we do when we seek the definition by dividing and explaining with various words. In this way, I say, error cannot fall in the Angelic intellect because, as we have said, through the definition of the thing, they know all other things that belong to it. This is understood regarding those things that are naturally ascribed or removed as a principle of understanding it, which is not so in things that depend immediately on <term>divine ordination: the specific plan or will of God that transcends natural laws</term>. Future things can exist within their own causes in three ways: namely, according to their possibility or <term>potential: the capacity for something to happen before it actually occurs</term>; these are called <term>future contingents</term> because they can equally either happen or not happen. Some other things exist in their causes not only according to potential and possibility, but also according to the operation and nature of the <term>active cause: the specific force or agent that produces an effect</term>; these cannot regularly be hindered from their effect, and these things occur by necessity. 

Others exist in their causes according to both their potential and the active cause, which can nonetheless be hindered in their effects; these are the things that usually happen most of the time. ### How Demons Can Speak in Assumed Bodies. Chapter IX.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial letter 'N' decorated with intricate floral scrolling and foliage motifs.</image-desc>

**There is no doubt** among Holy Theologians that demons can speak in **assumed bodies** <note>original: *corpi assonti*; temporary physical forms—often made of condensed air—that spirits were believed to inhabit to interact with the material world.</note> and with men, as they are accustomed to do with **Enchanters, Sorcerers, and Witches**; but let us see in what way this is possible. #### *Chapter III.*

## *How Sorcerers, or Witches, are accustomed to bewitch men, impeding them in carnal acts, even with their own wives.*

->Chapter V.<-

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial 'P' depicting two classical figures, likely cherubs or human figures, intertwined with decorative foliate scrolls.</image-desc>
These wicked **sorcerers** <note>original: "Malefici," referring specifically to those who practice harmful magic or "maleficium."</note> and **witches** can also cast spells on men, preventing them from being able to perform carnal acts, not only with prostitutes and other women, but also with their own wives. According to <term>Peter of Palude</term> <note>Peter of Palude (c. 1275–1342) was a prominent French theologian and archbishop whose writings on canon law and theology were authoritative in the late Middle Ages.</note> in the fourth book of the *Sentences*, at distinction thirty-four, they can cause this impediment in two ways: namely, internally and externally. Internally, there are also two ways. The first way is when they directly suppress the vigor and strength necessary for the strengthening of that member suited for reproduction; let this not seem an impossible thing to you, since they can also otherwise impede the natural motion of things. Secondly, they do this by prohibiting the sending of the **spirits** <term>spirits: in pre-modern medicine, these were subtle vapors or "vital spirits" believed to flow through the body to enable movement and physiological functions</term> to the members in which the motive power resides, thereby closing the pathways of the seed so that it does not descend to the sites and vessels of reproduction, or so that it is not discharged and sent forth. Externally, they can then achieve this either by means of **images** <note>original: "imagini," referring to the use of wax or clay effigies in sympathetic magic to sympathetically affect the victim's body.</note>, or by making them eat herbs, or through some other external thing; not indeed by the power

### *Of the deceptive operations of Demons, and of Witches. Chapter VI.*

Because we are to speak further below of the deceptive <term>prestigiose</term> <note>original: "prestigiose." In early modern theology, this refers to "prestige"—not in the sense of status, but as "praestigium," meaning a magical illusion, trick, or deceit that misleads the senses.</note> operations of the Devil and of Witches, for a more complete explanation it should be noted, according to Alexander of Hales <note>Alexander of Hales (c. 1185–1245) was a prominent Franciscan theologian and philosopher; his "Summa" was a foundational text for Scholasticism.</note> in the second part of his *Summa*, that "prestige," properly taken in its meaning, is nothing other than an illusion of the Demon. This illusion does not arise from a change in the thing itself, but only from the perspective of the one who perceives it, who is deluded and mocked by the Devil (or by another), both in terms of the internal senses and the external ones. Where, generally speaking, even of the human art of illusion, it can be done in three ways.

The first way is done without diabolic operation, and this should rather be called "illusion" than "prestige," because it is done artfully through the agility of men, who at times show or hide something from our eyes, as is seen in the sleight-of-hand <term>arteggiare</term> of these **masters of trifles** <term>maestri di bagatelle</term> <note>original: "maestri di bagatelle," referring to street performers, jugglers, or conjurers who performed "bagatelle" (tricks/trifles).</note>.

The second way is also done naturally without the power of the Devil, by the virtue of natural bodies to which GOD has given such a nature that they can, by their own power, make a thing appear in another [form]...

    *   *Paragraph 1:* "...feriſee, & prolonga; & quanto più huomini ſi dannano, & ſono deputati à gli eterni tormenti, & pene con eſsi loro, tanto più tardo ſi compirà il numero de gli eletti, il qual compiuto che ſarà, ancho ſarà finito il mondo.         *   *Meaning:* These authors [likely Malleus Maleficarum or similar sources] tell in confirmation of this that in a certain place there was a very famous witch (Malefica), who with just an external touch and at any hour caused harm through witchcraft and spells, and even managed to make children die in the mother's womb. In that place, the wife of a great lord being pregnant and having taken a certain midwife (Comare) for her care, she was warned by her not to go out of the city and to abstain by all means from speaking or conversing with the aforementioned witch.

Ahime che già hauete diſperſo; & come ella haueua predetto coſi auenue nel parto; percioche nō puotè partorire il ſan-"

## BOOK TWO.

...whether the storm <note>original: "se la tempesta" — this fragment likely concludes a question regarding the woman's power to summon weather at will.</note> would come; she asked for a bowl full of water; which, once it was brought to her, she told the man who was asking about the method that he should stir the water a little with his finger. As he did this, and as she spoke certain words, such a great storm immediately fell in the place that the man had designated—that is, in a woods near the castle—that for many years nothing like it had been seen.

They also relate that in the regions of **Swabia** <note>original: "Sueuia" — a historical territory in southwestern Germany, frequently cited in early modern demonologies.</note> there was a peasant, who one day was watching the grain in the fields with his little daughter, barely eight years old; and seeing the great drought of the countryside, and ruminating within himself and desiring rain, he said: "Alas, when will the rain ever come?"

The girl, hearing her father's words, said with simplicity of heart: "My father, if you desire rain, I will make it come soon." To which the father said: "From where do you have this power? Do you perhaps know how to procure rain?" The daughter replied: "Yes, father; and not only the rain, but I also know how to stir up the storm." The father said to her: "Who is it that taught you this?"

She replied: "My mother; although it is true that she forbade me from revealing this to anyone by any means." The father said again: "And how did she teach you this?" ## *On remedies in general, that is, how spells might be undone and dissolved; where it is discussed whether it is lawful for the true Christian to destroy them with other spells.*

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'A' at the beginning of the text, containing an illustration of a landscape with buildings and a tower.</image-desc>

**B**efore we speak of the specific remedies that correspond to the particular illnesses described above, we must determine if it is lawful for anyone to break a **spell** <term>maleficio: a harmful act of witchcraft, curse, or "evil deed"</term> with another **spell**. To clarify this matter, one should know that **spells** or enchantments cast upon a person can be dissolved and undone in three ways. 

Firstly, through the power and might of **God**; either that He destroys them directly by Himself, or that He grants a supernatural power and grace to an **Angel** or to a human to dissolve it. This is a clear and manifest thing; in this manner, righteous and faithful people sometimes destroy them through prayer and **conjurations** <term>congiurationi: formal commands or exorcistic prayers used to compel spirits in the name of God</term>.

Once all these conditions are observed, it is lawful to exorcise the sick and the possessed <note>original: "spiritati"; those believed to be afflicted or inhabited by evil spirits.</note>, and to place <term>briefs</term> <note>original: "breui"; these were small pieces of paper or parchment inscribed with prayers or scripture, folded and worn as a devotional amulet.</note> around their necks, or indeed to carry them with oneself.

Whether it is then lawful to resort to <term>Diviners; those who seek hidden knowledge or provide remedies through supernatural means</term> to undo a spell when all the aforementioned remedies have failed, various men have said various things. Some answer absolutely and without any distinction that one cannot resort to them. Others, such as <term>Silvestro Prierio; Silvestro Mazzolini da Prierio (1456–1527), a prominent Dominican theologian and demonologist</term> in the third book he wrote on the marvelous operations of Witches and Demons, and many others, make a distinction, saying: It is one thing to summon demons by means of Diviners, and another to summon Diviners—not so that they might call upon the Demon to assist in that outcome, but so that they might use their own knowledge and power to provide a remedy against these spells. This (Prierio says) I do not believe to be an illicit thing, even if they [the diviners] learned this through the Demon, provided that they did not summon him at my request.

In this last chapter, I want us to speak of the remedies suitable for bewitched animals; and also of the remedies that should be applied against the hail stirred up by Demons. For the explanation of this, it is necessary first to see whether it is lawful to <term>adjure; to solemnly command or charge a spirit, usually by an oath in God’s name</term> irrational creatures; to which question <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential philosopher and theologian whose "Summa Theologica" provides the framework for these arguments.</note>Saint Thomas responds in the <term>Second Part of the Second Part; original: "seconda secundæ," a specific section of the Summa Theologica</term>, at question 90, article 3. He says that they can be adjured, but by way of <term>compulsion; original: "compressione," meaning to constrain or bind the demon through divine authority</term>; and this adjuration must be directed at the Devil, who uses these irrational creatures to our harm. Such a method of adjuration is found in the Exorcisms of the Church, by which the power of the Demon is driven out and excluded from irrational creatures; because if our intention were directed simply toward the irrational creatures, who understand nothing, it would be a vain thing.
